pitch_detail.notes: Start up the white-streaked, S-shaped crack that passes a tree; the 5.8 is a few face moves about halfway up, and the pitch belays on a ledge just left of the crest. Above, easy fifth-class blocks and some tree-thrashing lead along the ridge to a big ledge beside a boulder. With a long rope the two pitches link; the lower crack seeps and can be wet.

A sustained splitter hand crack on excellent rock climbs to a tree; from there move right and continue to the next ledge. The belay is built on gear (a #1 cam fits at the stance). Some rate the crack closer to 5.8 for how long it keeps going.

The technical crux: a steep, awkward pair of parallel cracks that flare into a short dihedral. It is pumpy but there are rests, and small cams protect it well. Grades given range from 5.8 to 5.9-. After the cracks, traverse left onto the face to a ledge with a tree belay; long slings help, as rope drag builds from the traverse.

Climb back up from the tree to regain the ridge. The more direct line starts with a hard layback and eases quickly but is sparsely protected; the alternative is a short, awkward fourth-class traverse that adds rope drag. Easy fourth class then leads to a belay at the base of the next splitter.

Follow the 5.6 splitter up mostly fourth-class ridge, then make an exposed traverse around the right side of a gendarme. Rope drag is the main problem on this long pitch: extend placements before the traverse, or stop short of the gendarme if the rope is dragging badly.
Stem and jam straight up a pair of parallel cracks, taking solid gear, to a good belay ledge below the final wall. A clean, enjoyable pitch that sets up the widening crack of the last lead.

A crack that widens to 4–6 inches leads to left-trending, exposed 5.8 face moves on a blank slab before reaching a jug and the ridge top. The face section is widely treated as the mental crux: protection is small and sparse, so carry wires and the smallest cams (a 0.2-size cam is valuable here) and climb it carefully.

review.changed: Kept the same seven labels (1-2 linked, then 3-8). Grade chips reduced to single tokens (P4 5.8+, noting the 5.8-5.9- spread; P7 5.7; 1-2 5.8). Added lengths where sources agree or only one gives one (P3 55, P4 38, P5 26, P7 34 m); left out P1-2, P6 and P8 lengths because sources disagree (P6 110 vs 165 ft, P8 150 vs 85 ft). Added anchors only where stated (P3 gear, P4 tree). Crux flag on P4 only, which the route description names as the crux. Notes rewritten with direction, protection and rope-drag hazards.
review.other_findings: The stored route is 7 pitches; the route description and trip reports count 8 (P1 and P2 are often linked, which gives 7 leads). The route is 600 ft (about 183 m), which matches length_m. Grade 5.8+ is the consensus; some reports call it 5.9-.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin at the far end of the treed third-class ledge that slants up and right out of the approach gully. Climb the left-facing corner, a good warm-up on clean rock, to a stance just below a pair of left-slanting twin cracks.

Follow the diagonal twin cracks into a clean, inset finger-crack dihedral with a thin crux near its end. The rock is so polished it feels slick, and gear is small and sometimes below or beside the moves, so extra 0.2–0.4 cams are worth carrying. From the belay, walk about 20 m left along the ledge to the start of pitch 3.

Climb corners and yellow flakes straight up to the big left-slanting roof, then work left and up to layback, undercling and stem the steeply leaning corner crack under the arch. The crux is a tricky, burly sequence over the lip at the exit. A long, complex pitch. Treat the hollow flakes here with care.

The grade crux, and well bolted. Undercling a short left-leaning arch, pull out right onto pocketed face holds, and make a hard step-up past the second bolt onto the floor of the Supercave. The start of this pitch has some rock that calls for care. The cave itself is big enough to unrope and walk around in.

Leave the cave by its left side up a short, overhanging wall, aiming for a left-facing corner. The steep start is the crux and is considered harder than its grade; above it, the climbing eases to enjoyable laybacking that ends on a pedestal belay ledge.

Follow steep corners, flakes and ramps up the most obvious line of weakness toward the top of the wall. A harder direct line up the steep flake face goes at about 5.10c. The bolted belay here is where parties who skip pitch 7 start rappelling.

An optional short face pitch to a tree at the top of the wall. It is unremarkable climbing but reaches a spot to unrope and look out beyond the wall. From here, either rappel the route with two ropes or walk off down the third-class ramp on climber's left to the approach gully.

review.changed: Same seven labels. Lengths moved out of the notes into lengthM (40/50/50/20/30/56/15 m). P6 grade chip set to 5.10a, with the 5.10c direct line explained in notes, instead of '5.10a/5.10c'. Crux flag on P4, which is stated to hold the 5.11c crux. P7 anchor 'tree' stated. No bolt counts added: P4 mentions 'a second bolt' but no total is given.
review.other_findings: The stored grade is '5.11'; the route is consistently given as 5.11c (MP lists it as 5.11 PG13). One source calls it 'originally climbed in 8 pitches'; the standard description is 6 pitches plus the optional short 7th, which matches the 7 stored.

pitch_detail.notes: A long pitch of mostly 5.6 with runout stretches between pieces. The short 5.8 sections protect better than the easy ground around them. Choose belay spots with care: stances on this face can be exposed to rockfall from above.

Climb into the chimney system. The rock is grainy and below the standard of the neighbouring spires, and protection is spaced, so move steadily and test holds. Belays in the chimneys sit in the fall line of anything knocked loose, so tuck them out of the way where possible.
Continue up the chimneys on similar grainy rock, with some runout moves. Keep the belay out of the line of rockfall from the party above, and expect loose debris on ledges.

One of the better pitches on the route, on noticeably cleaner rock, ending on a large ledge. Above this point the route-finding becomes devious and the rock alternates between good and poor, so study the line from the ledge before continuing.

The first crux pitch: awkward, with funky protection, and some crux moves cannot be protected by gear alone. The second is exposed to a dangerous fall unless the leader places enough gear, but that gear causes heavy rope drag, so balance protecting the second against drag.

The second crux, as awkward as it is hard. The hardest moves have few, oddly placed pieces and cannot be protected all the way through on gear, so this is a pitch not to fall on. Only suitable for leaders solid at the grade.

A V-slot where the difficulty drops off sharply toward the summit. At the top of the pitch the route-finding gets tricky again; take care choosing the way to the top, and plan to carry all gear over the summit rather than return to the base.

review.changed: Same seven P1-P7 labels, no lengths (none published). P1 grade chip is now the single token 5.8 (was '5.6R (5.8 crux moves)'); the mostly-5.6 runout character is in the notes. Removed null grade/lengthM fields. Moved the rope-drag warning from P6 to P5, where the source puts it. Added rockfall-exposed belays (P1-P3) and route-finding after P4 and P7. No grades on P2-P7, no crux flags: the source calls P5 and P6 'the cruxes' but gives no pitch grades. Single-source for pitch-level detail, so medium.
review.other_findings: The stored approach text contradicts itself. It first describes the Kangaroo Pass approach, then says this route 'never cross[es] Kangaroo Pass' and goes southeast along the creek. The MP route page says to hike to Kangaroo Pass, drop some elevation and traverse to the South Face (2-4 hrs). SuperTopo gives 800 ft and 7 pitches; length_m 244 matches.

pitch_detail.notes: Start as for The Tiger, then step right over a small tree onto a ledge that runs right and curves into a long left-facing corner. Climb the corner to a pin-and-gear belay under a roof that traverses back left. At least one of the pins has pulled out, so carry several RPs and small nuts to build a solid anchor.

The first crux. Get established with awkward stemming off slightly creaky holds in the corner, clip the bolt, then stem wide left, place a quick piece and dyno off poor holds to a huge bucket out left. The dyno is very temperature dependent. Mantle out and finish on slightly dirty 5.10 to a small stance up and left with a snag; belay on tips-to-finger cams high in the corner.

Traverse straight left off the belay to a crack system hidden from view, and follow it to the big treed ledge that splits the wall. The corner is dirty, but the crack itself hardly needs to be touched. At the top, either climb the crack directly above a small snag or take the easier line right, which adds rope drag.

The standout pitch. Walk right along the ledge to the clean right-facing flake. Climb moderate moves up the flake, then make a puzzling switch right into a second crack past a thin seam. Power up that crack to its end just below a bolt, then pull through strong moves on square-cut edges that ease above the bolt. Belay from a stopper and bolt.

Make an awkward move off the belay, then face climb on good gear up the crack above. Layback a somewhat mossy left-facing corner with clean jams until a horizontal crack leads far left into the largest cave on the wall. Belay on bolts at the end of the traverse; protect the traverse for the second.

Aim for the hanging left-facing flake above the cave lip. Climb up and left on easy but unprotected ground to a horizontal, follow it right into a corner, and climb up and left past some hollow flakes to a small roof, turning it on the left. From a ledge with a small tree, run out easy holds to the first gear in a short corner. Climb the tree to a higher ledge and belay on finger-to-hand cams.

Traverse the ledge system left as it narrows until you are forced into a hand traverse and some downclimbing, then follow flakes and ledges to join the upper Ellen Pea. Belay on bolts shortly after the two routes meet. A committing pitch for the second, who faces the same traverse with a fall that swings.

Finish on Ellen Pea's upper line. Climb up and right on hollow flakes to the first of three bolts, then make steep moves on good but grainy holds until the angle eases. Easier ground leads up and right to a treed ledge with a bolted anchor. From there, rappel Ellen Pea with two ropes, or continue up runout 5.9 edges to the top and walk off to the west.

review.changed: Same eight labels and grades. Lengths moved from the notes (in feet) into lengthM in metres (210/40/190/100/150/105/130/180 ft becomes 64/12/58/30/46/32/40/55 m). Added stated anchors (P1 pins+gear, P4 bolt+stopper, P5/P7/P8 bolts, P6 gear), a bolt count only on P8 (three bolts stated), and a crux flag on P4 (the 5.12 pitch; P2 is described as the first crux and noted as such). Notes expanded with line, gear and hazards, including the pulled pin at the P1 anchor. No count added for the single bolts mentioned on P2 and P4. Pitch-level detail is essentially from one route description, corroborated in part by a later comment and the wall history, so medium.
review.other_findings: The description says the pitch grades are 'a little theoretical' because the route sees few ascents, and a 2020 comment notes the pitches above P4 are dirtier and see little traffic. The stored beta text says the original 1969 line used '1.5 billion pitons', which is nonsensical, and it names people as sources ('grades are described by the first free ascensionists as...'), which may breach the no-sources rule for beta prose. The FA field lists only the aid line; the free variation was climbed in 2015 by Herrington and Tepfer (per the overview).

pitch_detail.notes: Start in the obvious easy corner just left of Der Sportsman. Ramble up slabby ground in the corner, pulling over a few small roofs, to a two-bolt belay. The route then cuts right to head straight for the base of the summit headwall.
Move up and left to a band of overlapping flakes and roofs, step out onto the face, and undercling across into a secure stemming box. Belay there on two offset bolts.
Climb the corner to a short, awkward flare that holds the crux of the pitch, then continue to a two-bolt anchor. The flare is technical rather than strenuous.

Follow the obvious hand crack until you can step right to a bolt, then climb past suspect rock to a second bolt. The hardest climbing passes the next two bolts to easier ground. A blue Totem or a 0.3–0.4 offset cam is useful. Belay on the ledge at a two-bolt anchor.

Clip the first bolt, move left to cam placements, then work up a series of left-leaning seams. The moves are tricky rather than desperate, but the rock is poorer than on the pitches below, so test holds and place gear carefully.

The headwall: 5.11+ liebacking on imperfect rock to a bolt and a shake-out crimp, then a step right into a slightly overhanging finger splitter. About twenty hard, sequential moves on sloping locks follow, with only a few gear placements, before easier stemming. Belay on a single bolt backed up with a small cam; the pitch ends on the West Ridge.

The route ends on the West Ridge short of the top. Scramble the remaining ridge to the summit, then descend by the West Ridge rappels. The headwall pitch can also be reached by climbing the West Ridge and rappelling in to it.

review.changed: Same P1-P6 labels, grades and lengths. Added anchors where stated (P1-P4 two-bolt belays, P6 single bolt plus cam), bolts: 4 on P4 (the description counts a bolt, the next bolt, then the next two), and the crux flag on P6. Added a final 'West Ridge to summit' stage because the route ends on the ridge and a 7-pitch count includes the finish. No bolt counts on other pitches: P5 and P6 each mention a bolt but give no total.
review.other_findings: The AAJ gives 600 ft and 7 pitches on the southwest face; the stored length_m 183 (600 ft) matches, and the stored count is 6. The stored overview calls it a 'south face' route; the AAJ says southwest face. A 2024 comment (from a visit made before the free ascent) reported seeing no bolt at the top of the crux pitch, so the single-bolt belay should be checked.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb Peanuts to Serve You as the first pitch: a clean flake that begins as a wide, low-angle layback and narrows and steepens into a hand crack. A big piece (a #4 or #5) protects the wide start. The start is just behind a huge fir on the ledge, reached by the handline gullies off the base trail.

Continue up the corner, then take the finger-to-hand crack that branches up and left, the pitch's crux, to a three-bolt belay on a good ledge. Short but pumpy; grades given range from 5.10d to 5.11a. With enough gear it links with pitch 1.

The route's crux. Go up and right in a crack that starts wide and quickly pinches to finger pockets (11a/b). It meets a left-tilting overlap that begins as a hand pod and closes to fingertips (11c/d) for about 25 feet left, before turning vertical at 5.9 to a forested ledge. A 5.9 bypass goes up the low-angle ramp to the left instead.

Head up and right through the forest to a cave, then climb the short chimney on its left side; the 5.9 entry move is protected by two bolts. It ends at a comfortable grassy stance below a large corner. A newer alternative continues through the cave to Buckminster Palace and joins pitch 7 of Burt's Alpine Dirtbus.

Long and sustained. Take the lower-angle ramp and thin corner right of the big corner (10b) into the steeper corner above (11a). At its top, go straight up to another corner that trends left, mantle the ledge above and move up and left. For the last 10 feet, clip a bolt and make a single dyno to an incut summit hold.

review.changed: Same five integer labels, and the existing crux flags are carried over. Grade chips reduced to single tokens: P2 5.10d (the 5.11a upper figure is in notes), P3 5.11c/d (the pitch's hard section; the 11a/b lower crack is in notes), P5 5.11a (the hardest section; 10b ramp in notes). Added the P2 three-bolt belay, bolts: 2 on P4 (stated for the chimney entry), and fuller variations for P3 and P4. No lengths: none published.
review.other_findings: length_m is null; no source gives an overall length. Taking the P3 bypass variation drops the route to about 5.11a overall.

pitch_detail.notes: Jam the hand crack at the far left of the upper walls, where the approach trail arrives. It is often damp even when the rest of the route is dry; stemming off the left wall helps on the slippery opening layback. From the ledge, wander right and then back left over small terraces to a bolted belay in a right-facing corner.

Jam and layback the crack in the right-facing corner to the next bolted belay. It is a sustained, pumpy fingers-to-thin-hands crack that takes #0.75 Camalots nearly the whole way, so bring several; larger hands find it harder. Voices do not carry well between this belay and the next.

Make a bouldery move up and right around the roof, then back left into a right-facing corner; a variation goes directly left past a bolt on balancy friction that may be harder. The crux is in the corner, on delicate footwork and small edges protected by small nuts, so carry extras. It ends at a bolted ledge where most parties rappel or continue up Lovin' Arms.

review.changed: Same three labels, grades and crux flag. Added 'bolted' anchors to all three pitches (all anchors are stated to be bolted). Notes expanded with the damp start, the 0.75-size crack on P2, the left variation and small-nut protection on P3. No lengths: only a rough 30-35 m per pitch appears in comments, so none were added.
review.other_findings: The route technically has 6 pitches (the original continues left up a vegetated weakness), but nearly everyone climbs the first 3 and rappels or finishes on Lovin' Arms, so the stored 3 is the right working count. Descent note: the P3 anchor cannot be rappelled straight to the ground with a 60 m rope. Rappel about 25-27 m to a hanging three-bolt anchor directly below, then make one double-rope or two single-rope raps trending climber's left.

pitch_detail.notes: Start in the open book just left of a small clump of trees, about 150 ft left of and slightly above Easy Getaway. Climb the short broken corner, traverse up and right across slab into the right-facing corner split by twin cracks, and follow it until it slabs out. Continue straight up to belay below the treed ledge.

Climb up and left onto the treed ledge, watching for loose rock, then enter the left-slanting crack and tight, flaring corner. Gear is small (0.1-size cams and RPs) and fiddly. Do not pull on the chockstone and stacked blocks at the top. A 5.10 bypass goes straight up the narrowing crack before cutting left up a hidden ramp to rejoin the corner. Belay at a tree on the ledge above.

Climb a short, bushy wide hand crack to a treed ledge, then continue up the featured face and broken crack-and-corner system toward the clean left-facing dihedral above. Step right just before the dihedral to belay on a mossy ledge. With enough gear, pitches 2 and 3 are often linked.

The standout pitch. Step back left into the corner and climb the clean tips crack that is visible from the parking area, on thin, technical moves with plentiful small gear. Pull a juggy bulge and finish right with a short layback to a ledge with a large snag and a tree belay.

Walk down and right past a tree to the steep right-facing hand crack and layback corner, which trends right. Continue over a bulge and up and right through blocky ground until the angle eases, then belay. For the rappel descent, three 60 m rappels from a tree just up and left of this belay reach the ground.
Easy, wandering fourth- and very-low-fifth-class ground leads to the top of the wall. Most parties scramble it rather than pitch it out; it is often combined with pitch 5.

review.changed: Same six P1-P6 labels and grades. Lengths moved from the notes into lengthM (55/25/40/25/45 m). P6 grade chip changed from '4th class-low 5th' to the single token 'Low 5th'. Added tree anchors on P2 and P4 (stated), and the crux flag on P2 (called 'the crux pitch two'). Notes expanded with the start location, P2 gear and bypass, the loose blocks, the common linkups and the rappel start.
review.other_findings: The route is consistently graded 5.10d (MP header; the trip-report title); the stored '5.10+' is looser but not wrong. The FA trip report says the route was first climbed in 5 pitches plus a scramble, which matches the stored 6 entries.
